title: METAR Weather — 26 Global Cities, 2024–2026
subtitle: 958K raw METAR + SPECI reports from 26 major-city airports, Jan 2024 – Aug 2026
description:
# METAR Weather Observations — 26 Global Cities, 2024–2026

**958,338 raw METAR observations** (including SPECI special reports) from the primary airport weather stations of 26 major cities on 5 continents, covering **January 2024 through August 2026**.

## Why this dataset is different

Most weather datasets give you *daily summaries* or *hourly model reanalysis*. This one gives you the **actual raw METAR reports** issued by each station — the same observations used by aviation, and the ground truth behind most "official high temperature" records:

- **SPECI reports included** (372,730 of them, flagged with `is_speci=1`). Special reports are issued *between* routine hourly observations when conditions change rapidly. Daily-max temperatures computed from routine-only vs. SPECI-inclusive observations can differ by several degrees on 10–15% of days at some stations — if you've ever wondered why your computed daily max doesn't match a published record, this is usually why.
- **Full raw METAR text preserved** in every row. Temperature is pre-parsed for convenience, but wind, visibility, precipitation, cloud layers, pressure and remarks (including precise T-group temperatures to 0.1 °C) are all recoverable from the `metar` column with any METAR parser (e.g. the `metar` PyPI package).

## Files

### observations.csv (~100 MB)
| column | description |
|---|---|
| `station` | ICAO station identifier (e.g. KLGA, RJTT) |
| `valid_utc` | Observation timestamp, UTC, `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM` |
| `temp_c` | Air temperature in °C parsed from the report (0.1 °C resolution where the T-group is present) |
| `is_speci` | 1 = SPECI (special report), 0 = routine (hourly/half-hourly) observation |
| `metar` | Full raw METAR/SPECI text as issued |

### stations.csv
| column | description |
|---|---|
| `station` | ICAO identifier |
| `city` | City the station serves |
| `station_name` | Airport name |
| `country` | Country |

## Coverage

Toronto (CYYZ), Munich (EDDM), Helsinki (EFHK), London City (EGLC), Amsterdam (EHAM), Warsaw (EPWA), Atlanta (KATL), Austin (KAUS), Dallas (KDAL), Houston (KHOU), Los Angeles (KLAX), New York (KLGA), Miami (KMIA), Chicago (KORD), Seattle (KSEA), San Francisco (KSFO), Madrid (LEMD), Paris-Le Bourget (LFPB), Ankara (LTAC), Istanbul (LTFM), Tokyo Haneda (RJTT), Buenos Aires (SAEZ), Moscow Vnukovo (UUWW), Lucknow (VILK), Beijing (ZBAA), Shanghai Pudong (ZSPD).

24,840–53,862 observations per station (stations differ in routine cadence and SPECI frequency).

## Example uses

- Time-series forecasting of temperature at hourly/sub-hourly resolution
- Studying **daily maximum temperature** and how sampling frequency changes it (routine-only vs. SPECI-inclusive)
- Cross-city climate comparison over identical windows
- Parsing wind / visibility / weather phenomena from raw METAR text (NLP-ish structured extraction exercise)
- Benchmarking METAR parsers

## Provenance

Collected from the **Iowa Environmental Mesonet (IEM) ASOS/METAR archive** (`mesonet.agron.iastate.edu`), which archives observations distributed by NOAA and international METAR feeds. One request per station-year, routine and SPECI reports fetched explicitly, no interpolation — what the station issued is what's here.

Acknowledgment: thanks to the IEM for maintaining a free, well-run archive of global surface observations.

## Notes & caveats

- `temp_c` is as-parsed from the report; a handful of stations occasionally issue reports without a parseable temperature — those rows are absent.
- Timestamps are UTC; convert to local time before computing "daily" statistics for a city.
- 2026 coverage runs through August 1, 2026.

title: Weather forecasting at Vigo airport using AI
subtitle: Improving meteorological  models with AI at Vigo Airport
description:
### Context

Our aim is to improve the accuracy of the meteorological model with Machine Learning. To do so we need a database that contains input variables (meteorological model results) and output data (actual data from a meteorological station). Dependent variables are outputs of the meteorological model. Independent variables are measured by the meteorological station. The trained Machine Learning algorithm will take the variables from the meteorological model and forecast a meteorological variable. The meteorological model is a WRF model maintained by Meteogalicia, a public meteorological service from Galicia (Spain). The model has a resolution of 4 Km. We get the nearest points outputs provided by the model from the station. This dataset is focused on the Vigo airport meteorological station with ICAO indicative: LEVX. In the figure below you can see the ten nearest meteorological model points to de Vigo Airport meteorological station. 


![Vigo_airport_10points.jpg](https://storage.googleapis.com/kagglesdsdata/datasets/1206581/2059213/Vigo_airport_10points.jpg?X-Goog-Algorithm=GOOG4-RSA-SHA256&X-Goog-Credential=databundle-worker-v2%40kaggle-161607.iam.gserviceaccount.com%2F20210406%2Fauto%2Fstorage%2Fgoog4_request&X-Goog-Date=20210406T092656Z&X-Goog-Expires=172799&X-Goog-SignedHeaders=host&X-Goog-)







### Content

The dataset contains: 

1._Files (.csv) with the meteorological model: Format Lat42.22-lon8.63p10R4KmD0.csv when lat. and lon. represent latitude and longitude of the meteorological station. p is the number of nearest points from the station (ten points in this case). R is the spatial resolution of the model (4 Km in this case). D means the Day forecast. D0 represents hours H+1  to H+24 from time analysis (we use 00Z analysis of WRF Meteogalicia model). D1 represents hours H+25 H+48 and so on. Each meteorological variable ends with a numerical suffix representing the point. The nearest point is po and the farthest point would be: p9. Columns are meteorological variables forecasted and column time (every hour):

**lhflx**: Surface downward latent heat flux. Units, watts per square meters.

**dir**: Predicted wind direction at 10 meters. From North direction clockwise. Units are degrees. Unlike dir_o no variable wind is forecasted (no -1 values)

**mod**: Wind intensity forecasted at 10 meters. Units are meters per second.

**prec**: Total accumulated rainfall between each model output. In our case, every hour. Units kilograms per meter squared.

**rh**: Relative Humidity. Units fraction

**visibility**: Visibility in air. Units meters. Minimum visibility 26.028316 meters. Maximum visibility 24235.000000

**wind_gust**: Wind gust at 10 meters. Units are meters per second. Unlike wind gust_o always forecasted (no -1 value)

**mslp**: Sea Level Pressure in pascals

**temp**: Air Temperature in Kelvin at 2 meters

**cape**: Convective available potential energy. Units: Jules per kilogram. Check this [link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convective_available_potential_energy) for more information

**cin**: Convective inhibition. Click [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convective_inhibition) for more information. Units Jules per Kilogram

**cfl**: Cloud area fraction at low atmosphere layer. I found 1251 samples with values higher than 1 !! Perhaps, we wouldn’t trust this feature so much.

**cfm**: Cloud area fraction at mid atmosphere layer. Also, I found 37 samples with values higher than 1.

**conv_prec**: Total accumulated convective rainfall between each model output. Every hour in our case.

**HGT500**: Geopotential height at 500mb. Units m 

**HGT850**: Geopotential height at 850mb. Units m

 **T500**: Temperature at 500mb. Units Kelvin 

**T850**: Temperature at 850mb. Units Kelvin 

 **cfh**: Cloud cover at high levels. Units fraction

**cft**: Cloud cover at low and mid-levels. Units fraction

 **lwflx**: Surface downward latent heat flux. Units: W m-2

 
2._LEVX.csv contains METAR reports from Vigo Airport. Columns are actual meteorological variables and time (every 30 minutes). You can see more information about the METAR report [here.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/METAR)

**dir_o**: Observed wind direction. From North direction clockwise. Units are degrees. Value=-1 means variable direction.

**mod_o**: Wind intensity. Units are meters per second. All wind measurements are taken at 10 meters high.

**wind_gust_o**: Wind gust. Units are meters per second. Value=-1 means no winds gust reported.

**visibility_o**: Visibility in meters. Minimum visibility reported 48.280319 meters. Maximum visibility reported 9994.026301 (full visibility). Sorry for the decimal points. It´s a matter of changing units several times.

**wxcodes_o**: Present Weather Codes (space separated). 

**skyc1_o, skyc2_o, skyc3_o, skyc4_o**: Are Sky Level Coverage at several levels. Amount of clouds, roughly speaking. 
Categorical data. M means no cloud coverage.

**skyl1_o, skyl2_o, skyl3_o, skyl4_o**: Sky Level Altitude of cloud cover in meters at several levels. Value=-1 means no clouds cover.

**temp_o**: Air Temperature in Kelvin at 2 meters.

**tempd_o**: Dew point temperature in Kelvins units at 2 meters.

**rh_o**: Relative Humidity.

**mslp_o**: Sea Level Pressure in pascals

**fr_o**: flight rules: VFR, MVFR, IFR and LIFR

### Acknowledgements
The meteorological model that I used to build the database is maintained by Meteogalicia (a public meteorological service). Meteogalicia supplied a WRF model applied in the Galicia region (Northwest Spain). They use a THREDDS (Thematic Realtime Environmental Distributed Data Service), a connectivity tool between scientific data providers and end-users. We can get a historical model from Meteogalicia WRF [archives](http://mandeo.meteogalicia.es/thredds/catalogos/DATOS/ARCHIVE/WRF/WRF_hist.html).
The actual meteorological data are obtained from the meteorological station at Vigo airport. Iowa State University provides a database with the meteorological airports’ reports, check this [link.](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/request/download.phtml?network=ES__ASOS)

### Inspiration

I aim to find new algorithms that can improve meteorological model accuracy. We can set up supervised or unsupervised Machine learning algorithms to achieve our goal. The dataset would be a good start point
